title: How Far Away Is the Sun? The Solar System to Scale
description: One astronomical unit is about 150 million kilometres, but what does that actually mean? We scale the solar system down to a beach ball and a peppercorn and look at how the distance was first measured.

segments.text: Hey everyone, welcome back. Today we're tackling a question that sounds easy.
How far away is the Sun, really?
The short answer is about one hundred and fifty million kilometres.
Astronomers call that distance one astronomical unit, and it's the yardstick we use for the whole solar system.
But that number is so big it doesn't mean anything, so let's try to feel it.
If you drove a car at a hundred kilometres per hour, without ever stopping,
it would take you about a hundred and seventy years to get to the Sun.
A passenger jet at nine hundred kilometres per hour would need around nineteen years.
Light is a lot faster. Light travels at about three hundred thousand kilometres every second,
so sunlight only takes about eight seconds to reach us.
That means when you look at the Sun, which you shouldn't do directly,
you're seeing it as it was eight seconds ago. Now let's shrink everything down.
Imagine the Sun is a beach ball, about thirty centimetres across.
On that scale, Earth is a peppercorn, a couple of millimetres wide, sitting about thirty-two metres away.
That's roughly a third of a football pitch.
The Moon would be a grain of sand less than ten centimetres from the peppercorn.
Jupiter would be a marble about a hundred and sixty-five metres from the beach ball.
And Neptune would be a pea nearly a kilometre away.
That's the thing classroom models get wrong.
They have to squash the distances to fit the planets on a poster,
so we end up imagining the solar system as crowded. It's not.
It is overwhelmingly empty space.
Another thing people often get wrong is that the distance to the Sun isn't constant.
Earth's orbit is a slightly squashed circle, an ellipse.
We're closest to the Sun in early January, at about one hundred and forty-seven million kilometres,
and farthest in early July, at about one hundred and fifty-two million.
And no, that's not what causes the seasons.
If it were, both hemispheres would have summer at the same time.
Seasons come from the tilt of Earth's axis, about twenty-three and a half degrees.
So how did we figure out this distance in the first place?
Historically, one clever method used transits of Venus, when Venus passes in front of the Sun.
Observers in different parts of the world timed the transit,
and the tiny differences let them calculate the distance using geometry.
Expeditions went all over the world for the transits of seventeen sixty-one and seventeen sixty-nine.
Today we bounce radar off planets and measure how long the echo takes to come back,
which gives the distance incredibly precisely.
So, one astronomical unit, a hundred and fifty million kilometres, and about eight seconds for light.
Remember that number next time you see a sunset.
Let me know in the comments what other space distances you want me to scale down.
See you next time.
